text.p: Ending days of speculation, newsprint makers Abitibi-Price Inc. and Stone-Consolidated Corp. said on Friday they were discussing a merger.

The two companies said there was no guarantee the talks would be successful. Abitibi-Price is the world's largest newsprint maker, with annual production capacity of 1.84 million metric tons. Stone-Consolidated is the fourth largest, with annual capacity of 1.4 million tonnes.
Further details were not immediately available, but analysts said a merger of the two would provoke a much needed consolidation in Canada's newsprint industry.
"I think it's the new mantra of the Canadian forest products industry -- consolidation," said Jim Rowland, publisher of the Canadian Paper Analyst, an industry newsletter.

Toronto-based Abitibi-Price is widely held, although analysts said a Boston-based hedge fund may be its largest shareholder. Montreal-based Stone-Consolidated is 47 percent owned by Stone Container Corp., of Chicago.

After the companies' announcement on Friday, shares of Abitibi-Price were off C25 cents to C$22 on the Toronto Stock Exchange and down 25 cents to $16.25 on the New York Stock Exchange. Shares of Stone-Consolidated were up C30 cents to C$21.20 in Toronto, while shares of Stone Container were up 12.5 cents to $13 in New York.

Merger rumors about the two companies have circulated in the investment community for several days, especially after Stone-Consolidated tentatively scheduled a news release last Monday and then canceled it at the last minute.

If a merger of the two companies succeeded, Stone Container could end up as the largest stakeholder in Abitibi-Price. But analysts said Roger Stone, chairman, president and chief executive of Stone Container, might eventually want to sell that stake in keeping with his strategy to focus on his company's core packaging business.

A merger between Abitibi-Price and Stone-Consolidated would come with North American newsprint prices at their lowest level in the current price cycle. Many analysts expect newsprint to rebound from its current level of $500 a metric ton by the second half of this year.

Over the past year, most Canadian newsprint makers have cut back production to address inventory imbalances caused by weak demand for newsprint in North America and growing competition from overseas producers. Stone-Consolidated cut production at its mills last year by more than 150,000 tonnes.

Abitibi-Price and Stone-Consolidated own several newsprint mills in Canada and the United States. Abitibi-Price, which is generally an industry leader on changes in newsprint prices, has been trying to sell its mill in Thunder Bay, Ontario and at least one of its Quebec mills.
